No-op at book start and end, buttons disabled there.
- A progress indicator: chapter number and title, scene k of n in the chapter, sub-page i of m when m > 1. Quiet, small, Spanish.
- Music cue evaluation runs on scene entry only. Moving between sub-pages of the same scene never calls the scheduler and never changes the music. No IntersectionObserver, no scroll listeners, no reading-line logic anywhere. Keep the 06 scheduler (dwell, hysteresis, min track time, overrides, Cambiar track, Mezclar bandas, Orquesta / Piano selector, Just play Chopin) intact; only its trigger changes from "scene became visible" to "reader entered scene". - Pure pagination in core (`paginateScene(paragraphs, budget)`), tested: no paragraph lost or duplicated, order kept, a single oversize paragraph gets its own page, empty scene gives one empty page.

- Navigation reducer (pure): next/prev across sub-pages, scenes and chapters, landing on the last sub-page when going back, boundaries, jump to scene id, unknown id.

3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.

7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.

73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader uses continuous scroll. The unit is the scene.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion. Music changes at scene boundaries inside a chapter. No pagination.
91|- Reading position is the first paragraph visible at the top, tracked with IntersectionObserver.
92|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
93|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
94|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
95|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
96|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
97|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
98|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
99|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
100|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
101|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
102|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
103|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
104|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
105|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
106|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
107|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
108|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
109|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
110|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
111|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
112|
113|## Security rules
114|
115|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
116|
117|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
118|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.

6|
7|Continuous scroll is rejected. It shows the next scene before its turn and moves the music by scroll position.
8|
9|## Route and file layout
10|
11|```text
12|app/page.tsx                redirect to /leer/<first scene id>
13|app/leer/layout.tsx         server shell, slim meta, mounts music container
14|app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx server view, one scene only, generateStaticParams
15|app/leer/scene-page.tsx     client pager, keys, buttons, progress, focus
16|app/reader.tsx              music container, driven by route scene id
17|app/player.tsx              unchanged audio engine
18|app/player-controls.tsx     unchanged buttons from task 6
19|core/reader.ts              pagination, scene view, nav reducer, entry check
20|scripts/check-isolation.mjs post build scene isolation scan
21|```
22|
23|`/` redirects server side to the first scene id. Choice: one address per scene keeps jumps and the demo selector trivial.
24|
25|## Pure core pieces
26|
27|All pure logic lives in `core/reader.ts`. Choice: it already owns scene shapes, so no new module is needed.
28|
29|```ts
30|export interface SubPage { paragraphs: ReaderParagraph[]; startN: number; endN: number; words: number; }
31|export function paginateScene(paragraphs: ReaderParagraph[], budgetWords: number): SubPage[];
32|
33|export interface SceneView {
34|  sceneId: string; ch: number; chapterTitle: string; title: string;
35|  emotion: SceneSignal | null; pages: SubPage[];
36|  prevSceneId: string | null; nextSceneId: string | null;
37|  k: number; n: number;
38|}
39|export function buildSceneView(model: ReaderModel, sceneId: string, budgetWords: number): SceneView;
40|
41|export interface NavState { sceneId: string; page: number; }
42|export type NavAction =
43|  | { kind: "next" } | { kind: "prev" }
44|  | { kind: "goto"; sceneId: string; atEnd?: boolean };
45|export interface NavIndex { order: string[]; pageCounts: Map<string, number>; }
46|export function navReducer(state: NavState, action: NavAction, index: NavIndex): NavState;
47|
48|export function isSceneEntry(prevSceneId: string | null, nextSceneId: string): boolean;
49|```

60|

1|# Design: task 8 scene by scene reader
2|
3|Goal: replace continuous scroll with one scene view at a time, so the next plot turn never sits on screen and music changes only on scene entry. Branch `scene-reader`. This step writes only this doc.
4|
5|## Owner decision
6|
7|Continuous scroll is rejected. It shows the next scene before its turn and moves the music by scroll position.
8|
9|## Route and file layout
10|
11|```text
12|app/page.tsx                redirect to /leer/<first scene id>
13|app/leer/layout.tsx         server shell, slim meta, mounts music container
14|app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx server view, one scene only, generateStaticParams
15|app/leer/scene-page.tsx     client pager, keys, buttons, progress, focus
16|app/reader.tsx              music container, driven by route scene id
17|app/player.tsx              unchanged audio engine
18|app/player-controls.tsx     unchanged buttons from task 6
19|core/reader.ts              pagination, scene view, nav reducer, entry check
20|scripts/check-isolation.mjs post build scene isolation scan
21|```
22|
23|`/` redirects server side to the first scene id. Choice: one address per scene keeps jumps and the demo selector trivial.
24|
25|## Pure core pieces
26|
27|All pure logic lives in `core/reader.ts`. Choice: it already owns scene shapes, so no new module is needed.
28|
29|```ts
30|export interface SubPage { paragraphs: ReaderParagraph[]; startN: number; endN: number; words: number; }
31|export function paginateScene(paragraphs: ReaderParagraph[], budgetWords: number): SubPage[];
32|
33|export interface SceneView {
34|  sceneId: string; ch: number; chapterTitle: string; title: string;
35|  emotion: SceneSignal | null; pages: SubPage[];
36|  prevSceneId: string | null; nextSceneId: string | null;
37|  k: number; n: number;
38|}
39|export function buildSceneView(model: ReaderModel, sceneId: string, budgetWords: number): SceneView;
40|
41|export interface NavState { sceneId: string; page: number; }
42|export type NavAction =
43|  | { kind: "next" } | { kind: "prev" }
44|  | { kind: "goto"; sceneId: string; atEnd?: boolean };
45|export interface NavIndex { order: string[]; pageCounts: Map<string, number>; }
46|export function navReducer(state: NavState, action: NavAction, index: NavIndex): NavState;
47|
48|export function isSceneEntry(prevSceneId: string | null, nextSceneId: string): boolean;
49|```
50|
51|`paginateScene` splits by word count at paragraph boundaries and never splits a paragraph. An oversize paragraph takes its own page. An empty scene returns one empty page. Choice: boundary only rule keeps emotion uniform inside a scene.
52|
53|`buildSceneView` throws on unknown scene id. Choice: fail loudly at build time so a bad id never ships an empty page.
54|
55|`navReducer` crosses chapters through the global scene order. Next on the last sub-page enters the next scene at page 0. Prev on the first sub-page enters the previous scene at its last page. Bounds are no-ops. Unknown goto id keeps state. Choice: a reducer keeps every move in one testable place.
56|
57|`isSceneEntry` returns true only when the scene id changed. Choice: one predicate lets the container prove that sub-page moves never touch the scheduler.
58|
59|## Page budget
60|
61|Budget is 250 words per sub-page. Oz averages 35 words per paragraph and 8.3 paragraphs per scene, so most scenes fit one or two views and the longest fits about three. 250 words fill a desktop view at the 65ch measure without scroll.
62|
63|## Where state lives
64|
65|Scene id lives in the route and is the only source of truth. Sub-page index lives in client state inside `scene-page.tsx`, keyed by scene id so it resets on entry. "Enter at last sub-page" travels as `?at=end`, set only by the Prev button through `router.push`, read once on mount. Choice: intent stays in the URL because back and forward then land on the same sub-page.
66|
67|## Layout and audio persistence
68|
69|`app/leer/layout.tsx` mounts the music container once, so its state and the audio elements survive scene navigations. The container reads the current scene id with `useParams` inside `app/reader.tsx`. The scene page passes only the current signal down as a prop. Choice: params in the client container avoid threading ids through server props on every move.
70|
71|Navigation uses `router.push` and `router.replace` only, never prefetched links. Choice: no prefetch keeps other scenes out of the client cache.
72|
73|## What data reaches the client
74|
75|The layout receives slim meta for all scenes: `{ id, ch, emotion }` plus the chapter table `[{ ch, title }]`. The scene page receives current scene text and title only. No other scene text, titles, or summaries ship. Choice: titles can spoil, but the scheduler needs every emotion vector and the jump needs chapter titles.
76|
77|## Keyboard and focus
78|
79|ArrowRight moves next, ArrowLeft moves prev. Keys are ignored with modifier keys and while focus sits in an input, select, textarea, or contenteditable element. Buttons read "Anterior" and "Siguiente" and disable at book start and end. On scene change focus moves to the text heading and the view scrolls to top. No announcement. Choice: silent focus keeps keyboard users oriented without noise.
80|
81|## Progress indicator
82|
83|Small quiet line above the text: "Capitulo C, title. Escena k de n. Pagina i de m", with the page part only when m is above 1. Choice: chapter titles are the table of contents, not spoilers.
84|
85|## Music trigger and dwell
86|
87|Scene entry calls `observeScene(state, sceneId, signal, manifest, nowSec, env)` exactly once, gated by `isSceneEntry`. Sub-page moves call nothing. The 1 s `tickScheduler` timer stays to settle dwell. Selection logic is untouched. New config `sceneEntryDwellSec: 5` replaces the 20 s dwell for deliberate route entries. Choice: 5 s absorbs a double pressed Next but still cues inside the first sub-page.
88|
89|## Picture this changes
90|
91|Passage selection reads the current sub-page DOM as today and needs no logic change. "Ilustrar escena" takes the scene id from the route prop, and the `pickActiveScene` DOM scan in the panel goes away. Choice: the route already knows the scene, so scanning the DOM can only pick wrong.
92|
93|## What gets deleted
94|
95|`app/active-scene.ts` and its test, the IntersectionObserver wiring in `app/reader.tsx`, the stacked section divider CSS, and scroll only sticky rules. The sticky player bar and companion panel stay. Choice: delete the scroll machinery in the same task so dead code never invites reuse.
96|
97|## AGENTS.md and contracts edits
98|
99|AGENTS.md product rules: replace the three scroll lines with "The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry." `docs/contracts.md`: reader section becomes route per scene, slim meta, current text only; music section notes the entry trigger and `sceneEntryDwellSec`; image section notes the scene id source. `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` gains a 2026-10-27 row for task 8.
100|
101|## Scene isolation check
102|
103|`scripts/check-isolation.mjs` runs after `next build` in CI and in `package.json`. It picks a few scenes, takes excerpts from neighbor scene paragraphs, and scans the prerendered HTML and RSC files of each scene route for those excerpts. Any hit fails the build. Choice: built files are the real guarantee, since a pure view test cannot see payload leaks.
104|
105|## Test list
106|
107|Vitest beside the code, no DOM library. Pagination: order kept, zero loss or duplication, oversize paragraph alone, empty scene one page, never crosses scenes. View model: chapter counts, prev and next ids, unknown id throws, no neighbor text in pages. Reducer: next and prev across sub-pages, scenes, and chapters, back lands last, bounds no-op, goto with `atEnd`, unknown id keeps state. Music: sub-page moves schedule nothing, scene entry calls `observeScene` once, first scene plays at once. Isolation: pure view test plus the post build scan. Prefs and scheduler tests from task 6 stay green.
108|
109|## Risks
110|
111|Route params in the layout container can lag one render behind the new page, so the container must compare ids before observing. The `?at=end` param needs a Suspense boundary around the pager. Static output grows with 133 scene routes, so the build must stay static only with no per request code.

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
20|scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
21|covered zero or two times.
22|
23|## Music library
24|
25|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
26|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
27|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
28|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
29|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
30|`orchestral`.
31|
32|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
33|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
34|the Spanish display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
35|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
36|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
37|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
38|loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
39|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
40|`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
41|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
42|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
43|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
44|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
45|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
46|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
47|`startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, a non-boolean
48|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
49|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. A soundtrack with no
50|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
51|fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in
52|`next.config.ts`.
53|
54|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
55|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
56|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
57|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
58|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
59|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
60|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
61|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
62|
63|## Soundtracks and selection
64|
65|One soundtrack plays at a time. `MusicSelection = { mode, soundtrackId,
66|style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick, `soundtrackId` is
67|the home in `soundtrack` mode, `mode` picks the ranking rule. The style
68|is the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The initial
69|soundtrack is the one covering the most hand-labeled emotions, ties by
70|lower id; a valid persisted id wins. The session persists `{ mode,
71|soundtrackId, style }` in localStorage under `lectoria.music.v1`. On
72|load a stored style with no tracks and a stored soundtrack outside the
73|stored style fall back to the defaults. Storage exceptions never break
74|playback.
75|
76|In `soundtrack` mode each scene scores only the session soundtrack. When
77|the soundtrack has no track with the scene emotion, the scheduler borrows
78|the best same-style track for that scene only and reports `fallback`, so
79|the bar can say `de otra banda sonora`. In `random` mode each scheduled
80|select draws among same-style tracks with the scene emotion (or the best
81|same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within `randomTolerance`
82|(0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when it is eligible,
83|and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. Dwell and min-track rules hold
84|in both modes. The core never calls `Math.random`; the reader injects it
85|and tests pass a seeded stub.
86|
87|## Change track, mix toggle, style change
88|
89|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order, wrapping and
90|skipping the current. In `soundtrack` mode it stays inside the current
91|soundtrack first, then tries the same emotion in other same-style
92|soundtracks, then the best same-style track overall. In `random` mode it
93|ranges over all same-style soundtracks at once. A null scene cycles the
94|style set in id order.
95|
96|The `Mezclar bandas` toggle flips `mode`. Turning it off keeps the
97|soundtrack of the playing track. `requestStyleChange` moves the session
98|to the best-coverage soundtrack of the new style and picks the best
99|match for the scene inside that soundtrack, or the best same-style track
100|by score when the picked soundtrack lacks the scene emotion. It never
101|crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once with the normal
102|crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
103|soundtrack-change button.
104|
105|## Playlist mode
106|
107|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
108|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
109|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
110|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
111|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
112|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
113|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
114|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
115|restored selection. The mode is never persisted, so a reload returns to
116|emotion mode. The mix toggle and the style selector stay disabled while
117|it is on, and the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
118|
119|## Similarity and config
120|
121|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
122|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
123|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
124|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
125|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
126|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
127|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
128|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
129|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
130|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `switchMargin` (0.07),
131|`dwellSec` (20), `minTrackSec` (45), `hardCutMargin` (0.20),
132|`crossfadeSec` (3), and `hardCutCrossfadeSec` (1.5). Everything else
133|reads from it. Ranking ties go to the lower track id.
134|
135|## Selection scheduler
136|
137|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
138|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
139|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
140|timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
141|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
142|with the scene it belongs to.
143|
144|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
145|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
146|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
147|becomes active and the override clears. Then the best track switches in
148|only when it beats the current score by `switchMargin` and the current
149|track played `minTrackSec`, unless it wins by `hardCutMargin` (hard
150|cut, short fade). A second passes the active scene back through the
151|switch check, so a hold from `minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a
152|skip override stands: ticks return no change while it is set, and only
153|a new scene promotion clears it. A switch
154|reports its crossfade length: 3 s normally,
155|1.5 s for hard cuts. The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
156|after that, dwell and hysteresis apply with the override track as the
157|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
158|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
159|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
160|skip override.
161|
162|## Player
163|
164|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, the fade length for the latest switch,
165|the scene title, a skip flag, and callbacks. It owns two `audio`
166|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
167|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
168|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
169|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
170|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
171|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
172|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
173|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
174|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
175|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
176|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
177|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
178|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
179|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
180|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
181|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
182|
183|The bar shows Play/Pause, Volume, a Cambiar track button (disabled when
184|Next has nothing to offer), a Mezclar bandas toggle with `aria-pressed`,
185|and a style selector listing only styles that have tracks (hidden while
186|fewer than two qualify). A `Just play Chopin` toggle appears only when
187|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; its text comes from the
188|playlist label, it carries `aria-pressed`, and it shows the Meta blue
189|accent while pressed. It shows the track title with its emotion
190|label, the soundtrack name, and attribution when present: composer or
191|artist, license, and a source link. While the playlist plays, the bar
192|hides the emotion label and the fallback note. A fallback pick adds the
193|quiet note
194|`de otra banda sonora`. On manifest failure the reader still renders and

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
20|scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
21|covered zero or two times.
22|
23|## Music library
24|
25|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
26|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
27|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
28|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
29|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
30|`orchestral`.
31|
32|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
33|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
34|the Spanish display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
35|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
36|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
37|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
38|loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
39|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
40|`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
41|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
42|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
43|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
44|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
45|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
46|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
47|`startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, a non-boolean
48|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
49|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. A soundtrack with no
50|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
51|fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in
52|`next.config.ts`.
53|
54|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
55|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
56|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
57|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
58|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
59|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
60|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
61|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
62|
63|## Soundtracks and selection
64|
65|One soundtrack plays at a time. `MusicSelection = { mode, soundtrackId,
66|style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick, `soundtrackId` is
67|the home in `soundtrack` mode, `mode` picks the ranking rule. The style
68|is the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The initial
69|soundtrack is the one covering the most hand-labeled emotions, ties by
70|lower id; a valid persisted id wins. The session persists `{ mode,
71|soundtrackId, style }` in localStorage under `lectoria.music.v1`. On
72|load a stored style with no tracks and a stored soundtrack outside the
73|stored style fall back to the defaults. Storage exceptions never break
74|playback.

77|the soundtrack has no track with the scene emotion, the scheduler borrows
78|the best same-style track for that scene only and reports `fallback`, so

137|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls

2|name: ponytail-review
3|description: >
4|  Quality review of a change: is the logic right, is it safe, does it hold
5|  under real load, is risky code tested, is it fast enough, and is every line
6|  needed. Reads the connected code, not only the diff. Each finding is
7|  explained in plain English. Use for "review this", "code review", "review
8|  the last commit", "review my PR", "is this over-engineered", /ponytail-review.
9|---
10|
11|Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
12|Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
13|Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
14|This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.
15|
16|## 1. Understand first
17|
18|- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
19|  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
20|  if there are none.
21|- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
22|  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
23|- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
24|- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
25|  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
26|- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
27|  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
28|  that, and say which load you assumed.
29|
30|## 2. Look for
31|
32|1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
33|   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
34|   caller while the shared function stays broken.
35|2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
36|   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
37|   wrong order, no transaction).

7|# Type System Discipline
8|
9|Make the compiler reject impossible states, mismatched primitives, and unhandled variants. Prefer defining errors and special cases out of existence over proliferating handlers. For TypeScript syntax, see the `typescript-best-practices` skill.

2|name: typescript-best-practices
3|description: TypeScript best practices. Use when reading or editing any .ts or .tsx file.
4|paths: ["**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx"]
5|disable-model-invocation: true
6|---
7|
8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|

11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. 35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. 53|

55|

2|name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
3|description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.
19|
20|A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|
31|Examples: `references/patterns.md`.

7|# Type System Discipline
8|
9|Make the compiler reject impossible states, mismatched primitives, and unhandled variants. Prefer defining errors and special cases out of existence over proliferating handlers. For TypeScript syntax, see the `typescript-best-practices` skill.
10|
11|- **Brand semantic primitives.** `UserId` and `OrderId` are strings underneath but should not be interchangeable. Give each its own type, such as a branded intersection in TypeScript or a newtype elsewhere. Validate once at creation, trust the type downstream. If two arguments share a primitive type but mean different things, brand them.
12|- **External data is untyped until parsed.** RPC payloads, JSON, IPC messages, CLI args, config files, environment variables, database rows. Have a parse function at every boundary that turns unstructured input into the typed model. The **boundary-discipline** principle skill says where to put validation.
13|- **Derive types from authoritative schemas.** When a protocol buffer, OpenAPI spec, GraphQL schema, database migration, design-token file, or another file owns a shape, derive from it instead of hand-rolling a parallel type. See the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.

1|---
2|name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
3|description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.
19|
20|A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

7|# Prove It Works
8|
9|Verify every task output by checking the real thing directly. Do not infer from proxies, self-reports, or "it compiles."
10|
11|**Why:** Unverified work has unknown correctness. Indirect verification (file mtimes, output freshness, agent self-reports, cached screenshots) feels cheaper than direct observation. Acting on a wrong inference costs far more than checking the source.
12|
13|Check the real thing, not a proxy:
14|- Check process liveness directly, not indirectly through derived state
15|- Read the actual value, not a cached or derived representation
16|- When verification fails, suspect the observation method before suspecting the system
17|
18|## Script the check when you can
19|
20|The strongest proof is a deterministic script that re-runs the same comparison, not a one-time eyeball. Write the script, run it, and keep its output as an artifact a reviewer can re-run instead of trusting your word.
21|
22|Keep the artifact visible for the human. Commit it only for large or complex work where the trail has to be auditable later, like a big port or migration (the **show-me-your-work** skill).

7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.
